item.title: Search and Matching without Reciprocity
item.description: arXiv:2610.24230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study equilibrium sorting in the canonical search-and-matching model with Nash bargaining and ex-ante and ex-post heterogeneity. Under standard conditions for assortative matching under search, match surplus retains two properties of Becker's frictionless benchmark---single-crossing and single-peakedness---but necessarily loses the third, reciprocity. Instead, search generates consensus: intervals of types share the same surplus-maximizing partner. For such intervals, mismatched pairs are more likely to match, conditional on meeting, than perfectly assortative ones. Two forces drive this: with search, outside options rise less than one-for-one with productivity and fall more for agents with fewer suitable partners. Globally, upper contour sets of the match-probability surface are lattices below an endogenous threshold but almost never above it. This means that MLRP fails for some log-concave survival function.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Bonneton, Christopher Sandmann

item.title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
item.description: arXiv:2610.24819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.
item.dc:creator: Huseyin Yildirim

item.title: Coarse Revenue Guarantee in First Price Auction and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2610.24901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I study the coarse revenue guarantee (CRG) of the single-unit first-price auction with common values. The CRG is the minimum expected revenue over all information structures and all Bayes coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), the equilibrium notion to which no-regret learning leads. Identical play, in which all bidders submit the same bid, attains the worst-case revenue, and this reduction yields a closed-form characterization. The coarse guarantee is positive and increases with the number of bidders $N$. It lies strictly below the revenue guarantee of Bergemann, Brooks and Morris (2017) at every finite $n$, and the gap between the two closes at rate $\log N / N$. I extend the analysis to reserve prices, symmetric and asymmetric priors, other standard auctions, and an unknown value distribution.
item.dc:creator: Linchen Zhang

item.title: Monotonicity in streaming problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.25167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We explore the implications of the principle of monotonicity in the problem of sharing the revenues raised from subscriptions to music streaming platforms among content providers. We formalize various forms of this principle as several axioms for popularity indices, which generate sharing rules in this setting. We show that, combined with some other basic axioms (such as additivity, symmetry, or pairwise homogeneity), they provide axiomatic characterizations of focal indices for this problem, as well as more general families comprising them.
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Berganti\~nos, Juan D. Moreno-Ternero

item.title: Informative Imitation
item.description: arXiv:2610.25539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study steady-state equilibria of a sequential learning game in which each agent chooses between a safe action and a risky action of unknown profitability. Before choosing, each agent observes how many of the last $m$ agents adopted the risky action, but not whether they were informed or what their adoption costs were. We show that uninformed agents' imitation decisions can be strategic complements: the more likely uninformed agents are to join risky-action herds, the more informative those herds become about the action's profitability. When this complementarity gives rise to multiple equilibria, the one that maximizes the probability of imitation by uninformed agents also maximizes agents' welfare.
item.dc:creator: Nemanja Antic, Harry Pei

item.title: Winner's bliss: interdependent-value auctions with horizontal uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2610.25576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze auctions with interdependent values and horizontally differentiated bidders, where good news for one bidder is bad news for the other bidders. This generates a winner's bliss, reversing the well-known winner's curse: winning means buying an object that is more valuable than a na\"{\i}ve estimate suggests. Our main result is about the English auction. We introduce the ``own effect property,'' generalizing the single-crossing condition, to prove the existence of an efficient ex-post equilibrium. Regarding revenue, we show that with affiliated signals, the English auction yields no more revenue than the second-price auction, while independent signals yield the standard revenue equivalence.
item.dc:creator: Federico Echenique, Yu-Ting Ho

item.title: Balanced Social Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.25814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When is social learning efficient if agents have heterogeneous preferences over a set of actions? When myopic agents generate information only about the action they choose, efficiency requires balance such that all high-value actions are discovered. We characterize the value of policies that control the flow of past information to future agents. Under full transparency of past information, the probability of efficient outcomes is approximately one if and only if the prior and preferences are balanced and the log-likelihood ratio distribution satisfies a set of intuitive moment conditions. Noisy bad news is a canonical example. By contrast, approximate efficiency is obtainable on the set of arbitrary adaptive information policies if and only if the prior alone is balanced. Moreover, it suffices to use adaptive evidence policies which permanently and fully disclose subsets of past information. When the prior is imbalanced and approximate efficiency is unattainable, we characterize the value of adaptive information and show that it is uniformly approximated by the value of adaptive evidence as the impact of each individual signal on beliefs vanishes.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Koh, Ricky Li

item.title: Promotion Signaling and Signal Jamming: An Analysis of Job Title Inflation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Starting with Waldman (1984), it has become widely understood that an important role of promotions in labor markets is that promotions serve as signals of high worker ability. In this paper we explore the common and growing practice called job title inflation which serves a signal jamming role that reduces the signaling value of promotions. We first explore a two-period model and show how job title inflation can arise in equilibrium and increase social welfare both because workers directly value impressive sounding job titles and because the practice reduces job assignment inefficiencies due to signaling. We then introduce into the model an investment choice for young workers concerning human capital accumulation and show that job title inflation can decrease rather than increase welfare in that case. That is, when promotions and the associated wage increases serve as an important incentive for investing in human capital, the use of job title inflation can persist even though the practice lowers both overall efficiency and expected worker utility. We then consider three extensions: (i) a setting characterized by worker turnover; (ii) a setting characterized by a wage transparency law; and (iii) a setting characterized by heterogeneous worker visibility. Also, in addition to showing how job title inflation can arise as an equilibrium phenomenon that can either raise or lower welfare, we discuss the extent to which our theoretical analysis matches evidence concerning the use of job title inflation in real-world labor markets.
item.dc:creator: Yi Chen, Michael Waldman, Zhenda Yin

item.title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2610.24240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.
item.dc:creator: Mingyu Guo, Jiayuan Liu, Vincent Conitzer

item.title: Improved Approximation and Tight Competition for Simple Auctions
item.description: arXiv:2610.24973v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study simple auctions for one additive buyer whose values for $m$ items are independent. Write $\mathrm{REV}$ for optimal revenue, $\mathrm{SREV}$ and $\mathrm{BREV}$ for the revenues from separate selling and grand bundling, and $\mathrm{BSPA}_2$ for grand-bundle second-price revenue with two independent bidders. For independent regular items, we prove $\mathrm{REV}\le\mathrm{BSPA}_2\le2\mathrm{BREV}$. This establishes tight approximation and competition guarantees for bundling under regularity and answers an open question from Beyhaghi et al. (EC 2025). For general independent items, we prove $\mathrm{REV} \le \mathrm{SREV} + \frac{\pi^2}{6}\mathrm{BREV} \le 2.645 \max\{\mathrm{SREV}, \mathrm{BREV}\}$. This improves the previous approximation factors of $6$ from Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg (FOCS 2014, JACM 2020) and $5.2$ from Ma and Simchi-Levi (AISTATS 2021). On the lower bound side, we construct an instance in which prices for three disjoint bundles earn more than $2.11\max\{\mathrm{SREV},\mathrm{BREV}\}$, improving the previous lower bound of $2$ from Rubinstein (ITCS 2016). We also show that exact recovery of one buyer's optimal revenue by the better of separate selling and bundling requires $\Theta(\log m)$ bidders in the worst case.
item.dc:creator: Yichen Huang

item.title: Incontestable Assignments
item.description: arXiv:2401.03598v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study an information-based weakening of stability for school choice, using the evidence students may invoke in appeals. The model permits partial information about schools' choice functions and the realized assignment. A student has a legitimate complaint if, in every compatible state, she can block with some more-preferred school, and an assignment is incontestable if no student has such a complaint. We characterize legitimate complaints using an ex-post safety-set. For school-side information rules, under which the only admissible assignment-side information is the student's own assignment and all interim-compatible school-side states are preserved, incontestability is equivalent to respecting interim safety-sets. Stable mechanisms and Top Trading Cycles with responsive priorities are incontestable for every such rule. Pareto improvements preserve this robustness. When schools' choice functions are path-independent, all mechanisms that are incontestable for every school-side information rule, are non-wasteful, and guarantee group protection give each student the same attainable set conditional on her preferences and interim information.
item.dc:creator: Benoit Decerf, Guillaume Haeringer, Martin Van der Linden

item.title: Land and Infinite Debt Rollover
item.description: arXiv:2508.16002v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many analyses of infinite debt rollover omit productive land, whereas prior work argues that land precludes rollover. We show that when land's income share remains bounded away from zero, every equilibrium is bubbleless and Pareto efficient, ruling out rollover. If instead the land share vanishes and the autarky interest rate is below rent growth, every equilibrium contains a land bubble and permits rollover despite Pareto efficiency. Iowa farmland data show falling yields and converging district prices as price--rent ratios rise. This pattern rejects a bubbleless Gordon model but is consistent with a rational bubble earning the return on land.
item.dc:creator: Tomohiro Hirano, Alexis Akira Toda

item.title: Mechanism Design with Information Leakage
item.description: arXiv:2511.00715v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the design of mechanisms---e.g., auctions---when the designer does not control information flows between mechanism participants. A mechanism equilibrium is leakage-proof if no player conditions their actions on leaked information; a property distinct from both ex-post and posterior incentive compatibility. Only leakage-proof mechanisms can implement social choice functions in environments with leakage; efficient auctions and revenue-maximizing ones need to be leakage-proof. Second-price and ascending auctions are leakage-proof, while first-price auctions need not be. Appropriately designed Dutch auctions are leakage-proof and attain optimal revenue even with irregular value distributions. In multi-unit environments, leakage-proof mechanisms can attain the optimal Bayesian revenue even when dominant-strategy mechanisms cannot.
item.dc:creator: Samuel H\"afner, Marek Pycia, Haoyuan Zeng

item.title: Generalized Multidimensional Contests with Asymmetric Players: Equilibrium and Optimal Prize Design
item.description: arXiv:2602.21564v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study $n$-dimensional Tullock contests between two players with heterogeneous effort costs. We establish sharp bounds on discriminatory power $r$ ensuring that equilibrium is unique and pure across prize rules and cost asymmetries: $r\leq1/\lceil n/2\rceil$ when prizes depend only on the number of victories across all dimensions, and $r\leq1/n$ when they may also depend on player identity. An effort-maximizing rule splits the prize unless one player wins by a sufficient margin in the first case, and gives the weaker player a possibly zero headstart in the second. When both bounds hold, restricting prizes to victory counts alone can be costless despite unequal costs, but the percentage loss in total effort weakly increases with asymmetry.
item.dc:creator: Siyuan Fan, Zhonghong Kuang, Jingfeng Lu

item.title: Trading Frictions in Dynamic Cap-and-Trade Markets
item.description: arXiv:2606.03767v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using 2.8 million EU ETS transactions and compliance records, 2005-2022, we document three facts about the world's largest carbon market: each year, 37% of regulated operators do not trade, and non-trading is persistent. Purchases concentrate in the April surrender month, when returns are systematically high. Operator order flow predicts returns, concentrated among frequent traders. A model with costly market access, limited intermediation, and heterogeneous information rationalizes all three. Because access is endogenous, the frictions interact non-additively, shaping how efficiently the market corrects the externality. Staggering deadlines across four groups lowers the surrender-month premium by 58% without changing the cap.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Borri, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski, Xi Wu

item.title: Scoring Rules as Least-Squares Estimators
item.description: arXiv:2607.10145v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Kawada (2018) proved that a scoring rule represented by a strictly positive score vector is equivalent to the corresponding cosine similarity rule. The original proof relies on a direct analysis of the cosine similarity optimization problem. In this note, we present an alternative, simpler proof based on a basic least-squares characterization. For any fixed preference profile and score vector, the arithmetic mean of the individual score vectors uniquely minimizes the sum of squared Euclidean distances to those vectors. It then shows that, for any strictly positive affine representative of the given score vector, the optimal solutions of the cosine similarity problem are precisely the positive multiples of the arithmetic mean of the corresponding score vectors. Since the two arithmetic means are positively affinely related, they induce exactly the same social ranking. This result provides a transparent geometric interpretation of scoring rules and clarifies why the cosine similarity rule necessarily coincides with the corresponding scoring rule.
item.dc:creator: Satoru Fujishige, Satoshi Nakada

item.title: Effort without Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2608.03719v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I study how paternalistic concern for descendants' success affects learning about the need for costly effort. Each generation can use a demanding method or experiment with a less demanding alternative whose effectiveness is uncertain. Parents who underweight descendants' effort costs undervalue the savings that discovery would provide. On an explicit region of priors and preferences, paternalism removes a materially valuable experiment even though the relevant private record is truthfully transmitted. Relative to an aligned equilibrium attaining the material full-record optimum, the paternalistic equilibrium has greater long-run effort and observed success, lower discounted material welfare, and a less informative terminal public signal. Each sender obtains its preferred full-record continuation, so the comparison survives communication deviations within the same physical environment. I also study concealment as an incentive to experiment. A continuous-effort extension establishes that concealment and finite evidence production can coexist in an infinite-horizon equilibrium. Its welfare gain over babbling is distinct from the loss relative to alignment in the main result.
item.dc:creator: Georgy Lukyanov

item.title: Delegate Pricing to Algorithms: When Slow and Steady Wins the Race
item.description: arXiv:2610.11675v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the strategic design of learning algorithms in a canonical continuous-time pricing game. We introduce a meta-game in which firms select learning rates for a gradient dynamic, evaluating payoffs as the discounted sum of profits accrued along the entire learning path. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy driven by stage-game incentives: if the stage game exhibits strategic substitutability, each firm strictly prefers faster learning. Under strategic complementarity, however, an excessively fast algorithm accelerates the rival's competitive response, destroying transitional profit margins. Even though the competitive price is a dominant action in the stage game and convergence to this price is guaranteed, we prove that firms design sluggish algorithms in equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Galit Ashkenazi-Golan, Edward Plumb, Clemens Possnig, Yufei Zhang

item.title: Allocative Efficiency and the Returns to Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14969v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Innovation changes welfare by improving technology and reallocating inputs across producers with different markups. When producers choose markups optimally, an innovator's own output and price adjustments have no private value at the margin, so reallocation affects its profit only through others' responses. For an innovator small in its markets, the change in allocative efficiency is of the same order as its cost saving but does not reach its profit. A process innovator is paid its cost saving, forgoing its own and downstream markups on added output. For U.S. public firms in 2015, these forgone markups average 26 percent of that saving. For innovators accounting for 56 percent of sales, allocative efficiency rises or falls by more than a tenth of their private return. With estimated spillovers, patenting firms' R&D has a social return 6.24 times its private return.
item.dc:creator: Koki Okumura

item.title: A Note on the Stability of Monotone Markov Chains
item.description: arXiv:2401.11568v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This note studies monotone Markov chains, a subclass of Markov chains with extensive applications in operations research and economics. While the properties that ensure the global stability of these chains are well studied, their establishment often relies on the fulfillment of a certain splitting condition. We address the challenges of verifying the splitting condition by introducing simple, applicable conditions that ensure global stability. The simplicity of these conditions is demonstrated through various examples including autoregressive processes, portfolio allocation problems and resource allocation dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Bar Light

item.title: A Geometric Analysis of Gains from Trade
item.description: arXiv:2508.06469v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide a geometric proof that the random proposer mechanism is a $4$-approximation to the first-best gains from trade in bilateral exchange. We then refine this geometric analysis to recover the $3.147$-approximation guarantee previously established by Fei (2022).
item.dc:creator: Jason Hartline, Kangning Wang

item.title: Partition function form games with probabilistic beliefs
item.description: arXiv:2605.01521v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We revisit games in partition function form, i.e. cooperative games where the payoff of a coalition depends on the partition of the entire set of players. We assume that each coalition computes its worth having probabilistic beliefs over the coalitional behavior of the outsiders, i.e., it assigns various probability distributions over the set of partitions that the outsiders can form. These beliefs are not necessarily consistent with respect to the actual choices of the outsiders. We apply this framework to symmetric partition function form games characterized by either positive or negative externalities and we derive conditions on coalitional beliefs that guarantee the non-emptiness of the core of the induced games.
item.dc:creator: Paraskevas V. Lekeas, Giorgos Stamatopoulos

item.title: Human-AI Productivity Paradoxes: Modeling the Interplay of Skill, Effort, and AI Assistance
item.description: arXiv:2605.11350v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools are rapidly adopted in the workplace and in education, yet the empirical evidence on AI's impact remains mixed across different operating contexts. We propose a model of human-AI interaction to better understand and analyze several mechanisms by which AI affects productivity. In our setting, human agents with varying skill levels exert utility-maximizing effort to produce certain task outcomes with AI assistance. We find that incorporating endogeneity in skill development or AI unreliability can induce a productivity paradox: increased levels of AI assistance may degrade productivity, leading to potentially significant shortfalls. We construct interpretable measures that characterize when the productivity paradox occurs. Moreover, we examine the long-term distributional effect of AI on skill, and demonstrate that skill polarization can emerge in steady state. We identify an effort-skill non-monotonicity condition under which skill polarization emerges.
item.dc:creator: Ali Aouad, Thodoris Lykouris, Huiying Zhong

item.title: Congestion Games with Heterogeneous Valuations: An Optimal Transport Approach
item.description: arXiv:2607.03625v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In emerging urban mobility and logistics applications, such as advanced air mobility, electric vehicle charging, and shared service systems, agents with heterogeneous valuations choose among multiple outcomes while sharing congested resources. Existing congestion game and resource-allocation models, however, typically restrict either the structure of heterogeneous outcome preferences or the form of congestion externalities. We introduce a nonatomic congestion game framework in which agents have multidimensional heterogeneous valuations over a finite set of outcomes, with the population represented by a measure over the valuation space. We show that, although there is a continuum of heterogeneous agents, both Nash equilibria and social optima admit finite-dimensional characterizations. Nash equilibria are characterized by aggregate flows and outcome-level threshold vectors, while social optima admit a semi-discrete optimal transport formulation characterized by aggregate flows and strategy-level Kantorovich dual potentials. For separable utilities and latency functions $\ell_e$ such that $x\mapsto x\ell_e(x)$ is convex for every resource $e$, the social welfare problem becomes a convex optimization problem, and we characterize social optima through marginal congestion costs and capacity-dual prices. Our results provide a geometric characterization of congestion games with multidimensional heterogeneous valuations and connect nonatomic congestion games with semi-discrete optimal transport.
item.dc:creator: Pan-Yang Su, Negar Mehr, Shankar Sastry
